headline: Newfoundland and Labrador bill would allow 20-year cannabis licences
dek: Newfoundland and Labrador's Bill 33 would allow 10-year cannabis store licences, or 20 with a local production deal, and let growers supply their shops.
key_points: Bill 33 would raise the maximum term of a dedicated cannabis store licence in Newfoundland and Labrador from five years to 10, and to 20 years for stores tied to a production agreement with the provincial liquor corporation.
The bill creates related producers and related retailers, allowing a grower to supply its own or an affiliated store under such an agreement, rather than only through the Crown corporation.
It also lets inspectors and police seize phones and computers, sets new fine ranges, and widens who can supply criminal record checks.
The bill passed second reading and committee stage on 19 November, The Marijuana Herald reported; third reading and royal assent are still to come.
body: Newfoundland and Labrador wants its cannabis retailers to plan in decades rather than years. Bill 33, An Act to Amend the Cannabis Control Act, would double the longest licence a dedicated cannabis store can hold, from five years to 10. Stores linked to a production agreement with the Newfoundland and Labrador Liquor Corporation could hold licences of up to 20 years.

Finance Minister Craig Pardy introduced the bill on 3 November, and it passed second reading and committee stage in the House of Assembly on 19 November, according to The Marijuana Herald, which cited the legislature's records. The bill follows a five-year review of the province's Cannabis Control Act, in force since Canada legalised adult-use cannabis in October 2018.
## The licence terms

The bill text sets three tiers. A cannabis store licence, for a business whose main trade is cannabis, may run up to 10 years. A cannabis retail location licence, where cannabis is a side line, stays capped at five years. A store tied to a production agreement may go beyond 10 years, up to a maximum of 20.

The bill defines a production agreement as a deal between the liquor corporation and a producer covering cannabis produced in the province. The Marijuana Herald reported that the 20-year term is meant only for stores selling cannabis grown in Newfoundland and Labrador.
> A 20-year licence is close to a long-term commercial lease. The province is using it to reward cannabis grown inside its borders.
## Growers supplying their own stores

The larger change may be to the supply chain. Under the current act, producers' sales in the province run through the liquor corporation. Bill 33 introduces two new categories, related producers and related retailers. A related producer, under a production agreement, may sell or supply cannabis directly to a related retailer, and the bill states that the producer and the retailer can be the same person.

Producers could then sell in the province only to the corporation or to a related retailer, and retailers could buy only from the corporation or a related producer. The corporation itself would no longer need a separate authorisation to sell to retailers.

In practice, that opens the door to vertical integration for local growers: a licensed producer with a production agreement could stock its own shop. The bill does not say how many such agreements the corporation would sign, or on what commercial terms.
## Enforcement and smaller changes

The bill would let inspectors and police officers seize cell phones, computers, storage devices and digital video recorders during an inspection, and requires them to return the devices as soon as practicable.

It sets new minimum fines. One category of offence would carry a fine of $300 to $10,000 and another $100 to $5,000. The Marijuana Herald reported that the higher minimum applies to violations committed for profit; the bill text we read does not spell out the two categories.

Licence applicants could supply a certified criminal record check from the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary, the RCMP or another organisation the board approves, instead of only from police. Retail and production staff could give up to 30 grams of dried cannabis to another adult aged 19 or older, as long as they are not doing so as part of their job. Retailers would pay an annual fee set by the minister.
## Why it matters

Canadian provinces set their own retail rules under the federal Cannabis Act, according to our Canada legal hub. Letting local growers supply affiliated shops directly, rather than only through the Crown corporation, is a meaningful change to Newfoundland and Labrador's model. Long licence terms also make store businesses easier to finance and to sell, because a buyer gets years of certainty rather than a renewal date around the corner.

The trade-off is concentration. Tying the longest licences to production agreements favours operators that both grow and sell in the province, at the expense of stand-alone retailers on 10-year terms.
## What to watch
Third reading and royal assent: the bill's page on the House of Assembly website lists no dates for these stages yet.
Production agreements: how many the liquor corporation signs, and on what terms, once the law is in force.
Other provinces: whether any follow with longer licences or direct grower-to-store supply.
